summary: Teach the scale of the universe and the vocabulary invented to cope with it: a light year is a DISTANCE (how far light travels in one year, ~9.5 trillion km, at ~300,000 km/s), not a span of time; the Sun is one ordinary star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way, which is one galaxy among hundreds of billions or more in the observable universe, giving a nesting of solar system ⊂ galaxy ⊂ universe; and the distances step up brutally between levels (planets are light-minutes/hours apart, stars light-years apart, galaxies millions of light-years apart), which is why space travel needs enormous timescales and why we see distant objects as they were long ago (look-back time). Because the magnitudes are unimaginable, the core work is making scale tangible through proportional reasoning, powers-of-ten zoom-outs, and relatable analogies. The light-year-is-a-distance point must be taught explicitly because the word 'year' actively misleads.
misconceptions: A light year is a measure of time rather than of distance (the dominant misconception, driven by the word 'year')
The Sun is at the centre of the galaxy / the universe, or the Sun is special rather than a typical star
Stars in a constellation are close together / all stars are roughly the same distance away
The solar system, galaxy, and universe are the same thing or interchangeable terms (no sense of the nesting/scale hierarchy)
We see distant stars and galaxies as they are right now (ignores look-back time / finite light speed)
The gaps between galaxies are similar in scale to the gaps between planets or stars

activities.title: Fall backwards through the universe: a powers-of-ten zoom-out
steps: Starting standing on Earth, scroll/zoom outward continuously through the levels: Earth → Moon → whole solar system → nearest stars → Milky Way → the galaxy group → the observable universe.

At each level, read the live distance panel and notice the unit it uses: the Moon tagged as roughly a light-second away, the Sun and inner planets in light-minutes, the outer planets in light-hours, the nearest star in light-years, other galaxies in millions of light-years.
Watch each thing that looked 'enormous' — the solar system, then the whole Milky Way — shrink to a dot as you reach the next level up.
Find the marker showing the Sun's position: an ordinary star partway out along one spiral arm of the Milky Way, not at the centre.
Switch on a 'watch light travel' mode that crawls a pulse of light outward, and time how slowly even light crosses a single gap between stars.
activities.insight: A light year is a DISTANCE — how far light travels in one year — made concrete by the zoom rather than only memorised; the unit panel upgrades itself to fit the scale (km → light-seconds → light-minutes/hours → light-years → millions of light-years); each level nests inside the next; and because even light is agonisingly slow across one star-gap, space travel needs enormous time and the distant light we see left long ago.

activities.title: Build the light year from speed × time
steps: Work out what distance light covers in one year: start from its speed (~300,000 km per second) and multiply by the seconds in a year to reach roughly 9.5 trillion km.
Compare this to a made-up unit like a 'car-hour' (how far a car goes in an hour) to see that speed × time gives a DISTANCE, not a duration.
Rewrite the sentence 'the journey took 4 light-years' correctly, explaining why it is wrong, then say 'the star is 4 light-years AWAY' and state what that tells you.
Explain the two things '4 light-years away' tells you: the star is that far from us, AND its light took 4 years to arrive, so we see it as it was 4 years ago.
activities.insight: A light year is a distance built from speed × time; the word 'year' inside it names the time the light travelled, not a duration of the measurement. Distance and look-back time are linked because light has a finite speed.

activities.title: Scale models and matched-unit comparisons
steps: Build a proportional analogy: if the Sun-to-Earth distance were one step, work through roughly how far away the next star would be (hundreds of kilometres), feeling the jump between solar-system and interstellar scale.
Order these by distance and choose a sensible unit for each: the Moon, the Sun, the nearest star, the Andromeda galaxy — e.g. light-seconds, light-minutes, light-years, millions of light-years.
Order these by extent and state the unit for each: the solar system, the nearest star's distance, the Milky Way (~100,000 light-years across), the whole observable universe.

Mark on a Milky Way map where the Sun sits — partway out along a spiral arm, not at the centre, and note that, in the standard scientific picture, the universe has no centre at all (it is not expanding out from a central point).
activities.insight: Distances step up by huge factors between planets, stars and galaxies; matching the unit to each level makes the hierarchy explicit, and the Sun is an unremarkable star in one arm of an ordinary galaxy.

activities.title: Check and discriminate: distance, not time
steps: Answer the diagnostic: 'A star is 4 light-years away. Is a light-year a measure of distance or of time — and what does "4 light-years away" actually tell you?'
Explain: if a star is 100 light-years away, how long ago did the light we see now leave it, and could the star have changed since?
Identify and correct the error in 'the journey took 4 light-years.'
Sequence Moon / Sun / nearest star / Andromeda by distance and match each to an appropriate unit.
activities.insight: A learner who answers 'distance — how far light goes in a year' and can extend to look-back time holds the concept; 'it measures time / how long ago' reveals the classic misconception. Use these after the zoom and construction work, as a check rather than first teaching.

checkQuestion: A star is 4 light-years away. Is a light-year a measure of distance or of time — and what does '4 light-years away' actually tell you?
checkAnswer: A light-year is a DISTANCE — how far light travels in one year (about 9.5 trillion km). '4 light-years away' means the star is that far from us, and also that its light took 4 years to reach us, so we see it as it was 4 years ago. It does not mean an amount of time.
